kept.his:
I would also use topical magnesium chloride and consider topical DMSO with a known-genuine CBD preparation as adjuncts (a lot of CBD is fake or very dilute). Seizures come in all different types, and we have no study on whether CBD could be a rescue remedy for a seizure ([just anecdotes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RCxGSrUsB0Q)), even though we do have studies showing long-term effectiveness to prevent them: Purified oral CBD is approved for the seizures of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex. For focal seizures outside those syndromes, the evidence is mixed, but still long-term. 

And topical CBD hasn't been well-studied. There was a short 12-week trial done, where they used a CBD skin gel, and it did show that transdermal absorption works like oral CBD's but the dosing was too low, and transdermal CBD also doesn't get converted to the potentially more active form (7-OH-CBD) by the liver. 

As for DMSO, it did reduce seizure activity in a rats with temporal-lobe epilepsy, and we know it has several neuroprotective mechanisms, but it produced the opposite effect at some doses in an absence-epilepsy model. I'd treat it as a plausible experimental adjunct remedy rather than something to wait on while a seizure continues.

Psychological First Aid: The First Five Minutes

Anything that could let someone hurt themselves in the next five minutes takes priority, so get the car keys out of reach and turn the stove off, and move them away from roads and balconies, or pools of water for that matter. Letting them move around is fine, and pacing can help, but keep them from taking more of any substance. If they want to go confront somebody, that can wait. They're feeling overwhelmed, so dim the lights, and clear out the extra people around them.

Sometimes it can be helpful to remind them where they are and what's happening, since a trip can make them lose track of the fact that they took a substance which has temporary effects.

As the person helping, you want to play the role of the calm, caring anchor to the safe present moment, not the witch doctor guru who knows magic spells.

So don't try to win an argument with their visions, the entities they spoke to, the memories that surfaced, or whatever cosmic conclusions they reached ten minutes ago... But don't let silence validate anything harmful either, like a plan that ends with somebody getting hurt. If they're being attacked by a demon, let your care help them connect to love, which cancels fear. Hopefully they've been practicing that prior. Don't encourage them to believe they are crazy, impure, weak or broken. While many interpretations are possible, a therapeutic one would not be that they're being punished or failing the medicine. Don't force eye contact, touch, music, prayer, chanting, a confession or an insight on them. After they've slept, they may wish to talk more about their experience.

When you have a choice:

Physical safety: know the substance and approximate dose, review combinations and medical concerns, prepare the room, and decide in advance what requires outside help.

kept.his:
Give the Session a Beginning and an End
If you're planning a session, think through how it will start and end, and what happens in between, before you take anything. Rest and timing come first: don't begin already depleted, and ideally start earlier in the day, so there's time afterward for food, some normal company and most importantly, sleep. 

Set up the space you'll be in, and decide ahead of time what would make you call for outside help. Go in curious about what might come up, along with gentle intentions, not harboring demands for revelations, buried memories, good cries or spiritual breakthroughs. Sometimes people find that when they prepare to purify themself and open up to love, they don't even end up needing the experience itself. The work is already done. 

One woman I met in Kenya was going to take shrooms to fix her tobacco and marijuana addictions. Before she took the shrooms, she simply realized she was addicted to those substances because she was trying to escape anxiety. So instead, she let the anxiety come, and accepted the feeling until it left. Her addictions vanished, no shroom trip required.

If you're taking a psychoactive drug, though, know what you're taking and roughly how much, and look up what it mixes badly with and any medical concerns. If you've taken this amount before, that's a good starting place to understand how it could affect you this time, although people's sensitivities can vary from one session to the next, sometimes quite dramatically. If you've never taken this dose or done this type of meditation this intensely before, make sure you're not jumping into the deep end all at once. 

During the experience, the sitter (the sober person with you, not literally someone sitting on your face!) keeps you safe and offers you choices if relevant. 

As the experience winds down, give it some closure. Stop adding stimulation (I really don't like the MDMA protocols that include redosing, as it amplifies the neurotoxicity concerns). Check where you are and what day it is. Eat and drink a bit to replenish your electrolytes.

Jot down anything you want to remember before you forget, and let your body know the session is over with some gentle massage. Keep the rest of the day free, and the next morning too if possible, since your brain is still in a vulnerable, flexible, "plastic" state, and the goal is not to cement in worse new patterns than what you had before!

Anxiety and fear: grounding, routine, reduced stimulation, CBT-style reality testing, and therapy when it persists.

Sleep disturbance and nightmares: sleep hygiene, no more substances or intense practice, and professional help when severe or prolonged.

Derealization and depersonalization: ordinary-world grounding, exercise, nature, outside attention, less rumination, peer or family support, and therapy when needed.

Visual distortions or HPPD-like symptoms: reduce stress and substance use; seek professional support when symptoms interfere with life.

Social disconnection and shame: one or two safe humans, peer support, and no social-media crowdsourcing while raw.

Existential shock: write it down, slow down, and return to practical love before building a metaphysical system.

Paranoia or psychosis-like beliefs: professional support quickly, especially when beliefs drive unsafe action.

Somatic hyperarousal: gentle movement, breathing, grounding, and medical care for severe, unusual, or worrying symptoms.

kept.his:
Hearthwork: Taking Turns Lending & Borrowing Adulthood

Hearthwork is what I call my peer-counseling framework, which combines various other frameworks I'm familiar with. The basic premise is, peers take turns of equal length to privately listen to each other with respect and warm, positive regard. They don't try to interpret what's really going on, give advice, or fix the other person's life in the session. 

This is a "middle path" kind of relationship, that threads itself between ordinary friendship (so you're not "clienting" to your friends) and professional therapy (which gets saved for the more severe issues). Modern life rarely gives us anything like this, and your little one might really need it.

It also helps us with the borrowed adulthood practice. When you take turns listening with a good peer, on an equal footing, their warmth and the way they hold space for you are ideal for borrowing the Nurterer role and what that feels like. The Protector role can also be borrowed from the way they keeping what you say private, and the way you both stop when the turn's time is up.  

But they don't act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they're thinking, "Oh, I know what this is about," or "Here's what you should do." It's hard sometimes, but they agree to keep that to themselves during the session. Instead of telling you what to do, they might ask the right question at the right moment so you can hear your own Guide. There's also no pressure to answer. Then you trade places, and it's your turn to keep "Here's what you should do" to yourself.

look at what gpt is saying: Claude is correct about the basic electrophysiology of low extracellular potassium, but its proposed correction is still oversimplified. Your intuition about potassium being essential for keeping neurons stable is also correct. The apparent contradiction comes from confusing potassium concentration with potassium-channel function.

### What the experiments show

A particularly relevant 2002 study by Kuwabara and colleagues measured nerve excitability in a human patient during severe hypokalemia (blood potassium 2.1 mmol/L).

The researchers found that:

- The axons became hyperpolarized, meaning their resting voltage became more negative.
- A stronger electrical stimulus was needed to activate them.
- These abnormalities reversed when potassium normalized.

So Claude's central claim that lower extracellular potassium can make nerve cells harder to excite is supported by direct human measurements. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov\&sz=32)

pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov



However, that study examined peripheral motor axons during severe hypokalemia. It did not establish that psychological stress quiets brain neurons through the same mechanism.

### Why your objection is justified

A 2001 experiment by Gorji and colleagues investigated hippocampal neurons, rather than peripheral motor nerves.

They lowered extracellular potassium from 4 to 2 mmol/L and observed:

1. Initial neuronal hyperpolarization, as Claude predicts.
2. Subsequent repolarization and depolarization.
3. Spontaneous epileptiform electrical discharges, demonstrating that the network became abnormally active despite the initial hyperpolarization.

This is a direct counterexample to the simplistic claim that low extracellular potassium always makes neurons quieter. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov\&sz=32)

pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov



There is also a more fundamental problem with the article's proposed mechanism: blood potassium and brain extracellular potassium are regulated separately.

The blood–brain barrier maintains brain extracellular potassium at approximately 2.5–3 mmol/L despite fluctuations in blood potassium. Consequently, a temporary adrenaline-driven drop in blood potassium does not establish that potassium around brain neurons falls correspondingly. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov\&sz=32)

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov+1



And importantly, reduced KCNQ channel function can itself increase neuronal excitability and predispose to seizures. That is well established, but it is a different mechanism from lowering extracellular potassium concentration. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov\&sz=32)

ncbi.nlm.nih.gov



### What Claude got right and wrong

| Claim                                                                        | Verdict     |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| KCNQ channels help prevent repetitive firing                                 | Correct     |
| Adrenaline can lower blood potassium                                         | Correct     |
| Low extracellular potassium initially hyperpolarizes many neurons            | Correct     |
| Low potassium always makes neurons quieter                                   | Incorrect   |
| Stress-related blood potassium changes directly control brain KCNQ activity  | Unsupported |
| Eating potassium-rich foods restores KCNQ brakes during psychological stress | Unproven    |

The Brown et al. (1983) study cited in the screenshot is legitimate: experimentally administered adrenaline lowered blood potassium by about 0.82 mmol/L in six volunteers. But this reflected redistribution of potassium into cells, not necessarily a deficiency that needed dietary replacement. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov\&sz=32)

pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov



### What I would put in your article

**The Science:** Your neurons have electrical brakes called **KCNQ potassium channels**. They help prevent excessive repetitive firing by allowing potassium to flow out of neurons. Disrupting these channels can make neurons hyperexcitable.

Potassium balance matters, but the relationship is complicated. Low extracellular potassium initially makes many neurons harder to activate, yet experiments also show that sufficiently low potassium can produce abnormal electrical bursts in hippocampal networks. Furthermore, the brain regulates its potassium concentration separately from the blood.

**The Strategy:** Eat a varied diet containing potassium-rich foods, such as potatoes, beans, and leafy greens, to support normal nerve function. This supports general electrolyte balance, although it has not been shown to restore KCNQ activity or reverse stress-related neural hyperexcitability.

I would preserve your potassium-rich food recommendation as a nutritional strategy, but remove the claim that stress-induced low blood potassium directly disables KCNQ channels. The fixed daily quantity of potatoes and greens also need not be prescribed universally, particularly for people with impaired kidney function.

Bottom line: Your objection identifies a real weakness in Claude's reasoning. Its hyperpolarization claim is correct, but its broader interpretation overlooks experimental evidence that low extracellular potassium can also destabilize neuronal networks. Neither Claude nor Gemini has established the proposed dietary potassium → KCNQ → reduced hypervigilance pathway.
